title.en: 1. The formal command in announcements and service: -(으)십시오

head: What changes
The rule, with examples
rows: Words that already change completely work the same way

blocks.md:
**-(으)십시오** is a stronger, more formal **command or instruction** than -(으)세요. It’s common in announcements, signs, and service settings.

이쪽으로 앉으**세요**. (everyday conversation)

이쪽으로 앉**으십시오**. (an announcement, or a service setting)

items.tip: Please fasten your seatbelt. / an announcement
Please wait a moment. / a service setting

blocks.md:
**It’s direct, so it’s rarely used with people you’re close to.** With family or friends, -아/어 주세요 sounds more natural.

엄마, 여기 앉으십시오. (✕, much too stiff)

엄마, 여기 앉으**세요**. (○)

blocks.why: This is a formal setting like an announcement, so -십시오 is natural.
This is a polite request in a service setting, so -십시오 is correct.

blocks.q: 앉다: “이쪽으로 ___.” (write it with -십시오, as in an announcement)
blocks.why: There’s a batchim ㄴ, so -으십시오 attaches.

blocks.q: Which sounds more natural for a casual request to family?
blocks.why: -십시오 fits settings like announcements or service. -세요 is natural with family.

blocks.say: 승객 여러분, 곧 출발합니다. 안전벨트를 착용하십시오.
blocks.q: Read it clearly, the way an announcement sounds.

blocks.md:
**-(으)십시다** is the honorific of “let’s -합시다.” It’s used to formally propose doing something together in front of a group.

같이 가**요**. (among friends)

다 같이 사진을 찍**으십시다**. (a gathering or event)

items.tip: Let’s begin the meeting now. / the meeting’s chair speaking
Let’s all take a picture together.
Let’s all stand up. / an event host speaking

blocks.md:
**Be careful using this with just one senior person.** -(으)십시다 leads the other person into an action together, so it sounds natural when someone with a role (a host, a chair) says it to a group. For a single senior person, -(으)실까요? is softer.

할머니, 같이 가십시다. (△, feels like directing someone senior)

할머니, 같이 가**실까요**? (○, much softer)

blocks.why: The person leading the meeting is formally proposing this to the group, so -십시다 is correct.
This is leading a group at an event to do something together, so it’s -십시다.

blocks.q: 찍다: “다 같이 사진을 ___.” Write the honorific for proposing an action.
blocks.why: There’s a batchim ㄱ, so -으십시다 attaches.

blocks.q: Which is softer when kindly proposing something to a single grandmother?
blocks.why: -십시다 feels like leading someone. For one senior person, -(으)실까요? is softer.

blocks.say: 자, 그럼 다 같이 박수를 치십시다!
blocks.q: Read it energetically, like an event host.

title.en: 3. Humble words that lower yourself, 드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다

head: What changes
Example
rows: 저는, 저희 (humble forms of 나, 우리)
주다, when giving to someone senior
데리고 가다, when accompanying someone senior

blocks.md:
-(으)시-, which you’ve learned so far, honors **the subject of the sentence** (someone senior). Humble expressions do the opposite: they **lower yourself, the speaker**, to indirectly honor the other person.

할머니께서 저에게 선물을 **주세요**. (the subject is 할머니, subject honorification)

제가 할머니께 선물을 **드려요**. (the subject is “I,” but since the receiver is 할머니, a humble word is used)

items.tip: Let me introduce my parents. / both 저희 and 드리다 are humble forms
I’ll ask the teacher and get back to you.
I will see you tomorrow afternoon. / a polite greeting
I took Grandma to the hospital.

blocks.md:
**They honor different people.** -(으)시- honors the subject of the sentence; humble expressions honor the person on the receiving end (the object) or the listener.

제가 할머니를 모시고 가세요. (✕, the subject is “I,” but -세요 was attached)

제가 할머니를 모시고 **가요**. (○, 모시다 is already a humble word, so -시- isn’t added again)

blocks.meaning: Teacher, let me carry your bag for you.
blocks.why: This is done for someone senior, so 드리다 is used instead of 주다.

blocks.meaning: I will see you tomorrow at 2pm.
blocks.why: This means meeting someone senior, so 뵙다 is used instead of 보다.
This is asking someone senior, so 여쭙다 is used.

blocks.q: Which one uses a humble expression correctly?
blocks.why: I am giving something to someone senior, so 드리다 is correct. The first sentence wrongly attaches -세요 to “I” (the subject); the third has 할머니 giving, which should instead be -세요, not 드리다.

blocks.q: Both 모시다 and -겠습니다 are polite here. Read it clearly.

head: Situation
Expression
Example
rows: A formal proposal to a group
Lowering yourself to honor someone else

blocks.h: Four questions are all you need
blocks.md:
**① Who is this about?**: If the subject is someone senior, -(으)시- goes in.

**② When?**, Right now, keep it as is; already happened, add -셨-.

**③ How formal is the setting?**, Everyday conversation: -어요. An announcement or service setting: -ㅂ니다/-십시오.

**④ What am I doing for someone senior?**, Giving, asking, or meeting them calls for a humble expression (드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다).

items.tip: humble (드리다) / what I’m doing is for Grandma

items.ch: 손님 여러분, 곧 문이 닫힙니다. 안전선 밖으로 나와 주십시오.

blocks.md:
**Subject honorification and humble expressions can appear in the same sentence.** If the subject is someone senior, use -시-. If I’m doing something for someone senior, use a humble word.

제가 할머니를 모시고 병원에 **가요**. (the humble word 모시다, I don’t also add -시-)

할머니께서 병원에 **가세요**. (the subject is 할머니, here it does take -시-)

blocks.meaning: Grandma, let me carry your bag.
blocks.why: This is done for someone senior, so 드리다 is used.
This is a formal setting like an announcement, so -십시오 is correct.

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “같이 사진 찍어요” as an event host proposing it to the group.
blocks.hint: This is someone leading an event, so use -으십시다

blocks.q: Rewrite the basic sentence “선생님께 물어볼게요” using a humble expression.
blocks.hint: This is asking someone senior, so use 여쭙다 instead of 묻다

blocks.why: The subject is “I,” but -세요 was attached. Since this is given to someone senior, “선물을 드려요” is correct.

blocks.q: Put together “할머니, 제가 짐을 들어 드릴게요.”

blocks.say: 제가 할머니를 모시고 병원에 다녀오겠습니다. 걱정하지 마십시오.
blocks.q: A humble word (모시다) and a formal command (-십시오) appear one after another here.
